Chapter 7 • Metric

7.3 The Levi-Civita Connection

  • The geodesic equation (7.1) has the form of the autoparallel equation (6.1), with the connection coefficient functions replaced by the Christoffel symbols of \(g\) w.r.t. \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\), \begin{equation} \boxed{ \big( \Gamma^{\text{LC}}_\mathscr{X} \big)^k_{ji} \coloneqq \frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{km} \big( \partial_i g_{mj} + \partial_j g_{mi} - \partial_m g_{ij} \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}). } \tag{7.2} \end{equation} The Levi-Civita connection \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) is the connection whose connection coefficient functions are, in every chart, the Christoffel symbols. With this choice, (6.1) becomes (7.1) term by term, so the straight curves of \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) are the extremal curves of the length. Moreover, exchanging \(i \leftrightarrow j\) swaps the first two terms of the Christoffel symbols and leaves the third invariant (\(g_{ij} = g_{ji}\)), so \((\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ji} = (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ij}\), and \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) is torsion free, \(\mathtt{T}^k_{ji} = (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ij} - (\Gamma_\mathscr{X})^k_{ji} = 0\).

  • A connection \(\nabla\) is metric compatible if \(\nabla_\mathcal{X} g = 0\) for all \(\mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\). In a chart, \begin{equation} (\nabla_{\partial x_k} g)_{ij} = \partial_k g_{ij} - \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} - \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} . \tag{7.3} \end{equation} As torsion freeness, metric compatibility of \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) follows from its definition: inserting the Christoffel symbols, \(\Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} = \frac{1}{2} \big( \partial_k g_{ji} + \partial_i g_{jk} - \partial_j g_{ki} \big)\) and \(\Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} = \frac{1}{2} \big( \partial_k g_{ij} + \partial_j g_{ik} - \partial_i g_{kj} \big)\), whose sum is \(\partial_k g_{ij}\). Conversely, the two properties characterize it:

    Theorem (Levi-Civita). \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) is the only torsion-free, metric-compatible connection on a metric manifold7.

  • By metric compatibility, parallel transport with \(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\) preserves \(g\): for vector fields \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\), \(\mathcal{Y}_\gamma\) along \(\gamma\), \(\frac{d}{d\lambda} \, g(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) = g(\nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma) + g(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{Y}_\gamma)\) (Appendix B.18.5). Along an autoparallelly transported curve, \(g(v_\gamma, v_\gamma)\), and hence \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma\) and \(s_\gamma\), are therefore constant. Its autoparallelly transported curves with \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma \neq 0\) are thus exactly the constant-speed geodesics, while those with \(\textrm{\runic ᛇ}_\gamma = 0\), not covered by the variational definition, are called null geodesics. For a general connection the two notions differ: autoparallels depend on \(\nabla\), geodesics only on \(g\).

7

See Appendix B.17 for the proof, and for the fact that the Christoffel symbols of overlapping charts define the same connection.
